doc.title: Ted Piltzecker interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 10, 2019

title: Political polarization and his views on the administration
summary: Piltzecker describes political polarization in everyday life and states his opposition to the current administration.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: Well I know you have to be on your way to your next gig in this gig economy, but I do want to give you an opportunity — I’ll bet you have an opinion about the current state of affairs in our country in a broad sense if you feel like talking about it for a minute.

Well this is very interesting because you always — you know we go to these dinner parties or cocktail parties or just happen to meet somebody at Starbucks and you do this dance until you find out what political side the person you’re addressing is on. And you’re afraid this is a trepidation, oh my God, oh no, I don’t want to blow this relationship, I don’t want — they’re going to hate me — or great, I’m going to have a compadre where we can talk about how horrible things are. So it happens every day because of the intense polarization we have today. Every day. It happened to me this morning with, you know, and people that I really love and really respected, I didn’t know, and because time was limited I decided we’re not going to go there. Like I was talking about earlier in the plane. You don’t want to spoil, you don’t want to cause a tense situation. So now here I am, I don’t know if this is an audience, but you give me a chance to express my political views. I will, and I am not in any way happy with this administration. The sooner we get back to the values, the real values of this country, which means honoring the constitution and the separation of powers and, and when you look at — you give me a soapbox but the, in terms of our environment for our grandchildren and their kids, rather than the corporate dollar. Those types of things are vitally important. We have usurped so much of our power and our moral — the morality, because of what we stand for that had sway that has been just so quickly spent and squandered. So there I go with my opinions about this thing. Maybe I’ve made an enemy of you. I don’t know. But you asked me. That’s how I feel. And then sometimes, oh great, when we feel the same we can talk about it. But I find it deeply troubling. And I think if I didn’t have children I’d say hey may I’ve been lucky, I’ve had a wonderful experience, I’ve lived a good life, I’ll be checking out pretty soon and thank you very much and it’s been great. I care about the future generations and I do care about this American experiment and it’s one empire, it’s one civilization in four thousand years of stuff it’s been going on. Nothing lasts forever. I know all that. But I do care about it and it’s troubling to see things go south at this point. I think it’s vitally important that we act pretty soon and I encourage all of you, whoever reads this, it might be past election time, or sees this thing, I hope you do vote. For about six months before an election I go to school every day with —I don’t preach but I just have a shirt that says “Vote.”
Well your sentiment has my vote. All right?
Well thank you. And I hope I didn’t make any enemies and if I did forgive me, sir.
